subsection: 2. Water-soluble vitamins C, B12 and folate

notes.b: Vitamin C, vitamin B12 and folate are water-soluble vitamins, so they behave differently from vitamins that dissolve in fat. Knowing this explains why they are needed every day and why cooking can ruin them.
points: Water-soluble vitamins (the B group and C) dissolve in water and are not stored in useful amounts in the body. Any excess is lost in urine, so they are needed regularly in the diet.
The exception is vitamin B12, which the liver stores, so a store builds up that can last for several years.
Because they dissolve in water, these vitamins are lost into cooking water and are easily destroyed during storage, preparation and cooking.

The RDA (recommended daily allowance) is the daily amount of a nutrient that meets the needs of almost everyone in a group. It varies with age, sex, pregnancy and breastfeeding, and smokers are advised more vitamin C.
notes.tip: Exams use gap-fill and true or false questions on vitamin C and iron absorption, so learn the basic features of water-soluble vitamins along with the specific vitamins.

notes.b: Vitamin C is the most-asked vitamin in the exam, and it comes mainly from fruit and vegetables. Fresh, raw and in-season produce has the most.
points: Citrus fruit (oranges, lemons, grapefruit), blackcurrants, rosehips, kiwi fruit and strawberries are rich sources of vitamin C.
Peppers, broccoli, sprouts, cabbage, tomatoes, new potatoes and peas are good vegetable sources.
Fresh fruit juices and smoothies, and fortified drinks, also supply vitamin C, and a supplement can too. Any fruit or vegetable is accepted as a source in an answer.
notes.tip: When asked to name a source, give a specific food such as citrus fruit, blackcurrants, peppers or kiwi.

notes.b: Vitamin C does several different jobs in the body, and exam questions usually ask for two or three of them. The key one is collagen, because so many other effects follow from it.
points: Vitamin C is needed to make collagen, the protein of connective tissue that gives strength to skin, blood vessels, gums, cartilage, bones and teeth.
By supporting collagen formation, vitamin C speeds up the healing of wounds, because new tissue can be built.
Vitamin C aids iron absorption. It converts non-haem iron (the iron in plant foods) from the ferric form (Fe³⁺) to the ferrous form (Fe²⁺), which is absorbed more readily.
Vitamin C also aids calcium absorption, which marking schemes accept.
Vitamin C is an antioxidant: it neutralises free radicals (damaging particles) and so protects cells from damage.
Vitamin C supports the immune system, helping the body resist infection, and it prevents scurvy.
notes.tip: Say that vitamin C changes ferric iron (Fe³⁺) to ferrous iron (Fe²⁺), not that it turns iron into haem iron. It does not directly strengthen bones: it makes the collagen framework that bone and teeth are built on. Don't write that it cures or prevents colds.

notes.b: If the diet lacks vitamin C for a long time, collagen cannot be made properly and the body's tissues start to fail. The deficiency disease is scurvy.
points: Scurvy develops after a severe and prolonged lack of vitamin C in the diet.
Weak collagen causes bleeding, sore and swollen gums, loose teeth, easy bruising and painful joints.
Wounds heal slowly because new tissue cannot be formed properly.
Reduced iron absorption can lead to anaemia, with tiredness and pale skin.
The body becomes more susceptible to infection because its resistance is lowered.
notes.tip: Scurvy is the vitamin C disease; beri-beri is B1, pellagra is niacin and rickets is D, and past papers test this matching. For a deficiency answer give scurvy, bleeding gums, bruising, slow healing, anaemia and infections.

notes.h: Retaining vitamin C when preparing and cooking
notes.b: Vitamin C is easily lost, but the loss depends on method and time. Cooking does not destroy all of it: steaming, microwaving and short cooking keep most.
points: Buy fresh produce and use it quickly, and eat it raw where possible.
Wash vegetables before cutting rather than soaking them, prepare them just before cooking and cut them in large pieces, so less of the surface is exposed.
Cook in a little boiling water for a short time with the lid on, or steam, microwave or stir-fry, so less vitamin C dissolves or is destroyed.
Do not use bicarbonate of soda or copper pans, which destroy the vitamin.
Serve at once rather than keeping the food hot, and use the cooking water in soups and sauces to recover the vitamin that dissolved into it.
notes.tip: Questions on retaining vitamin C expect: use fresh, avoid soaking, cook briefly, use minimum water, put the lid on, and avoid bicarbonate of soda and copper pans.

notes.h: Properties of vitamin C (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Ascorbic acid is a very unstable vitamin, and its properties explain every rule for keeping it in food. Higher Level answers on vitamin C add these properties to sources, functions and deficiency.
points: Vitamin C is a white, crystalline, acidic substance with a sweet-sour taste, and it is very soluble in water.
Because it is water-soluble, vitamin C is lost into cooking water when vegetables are boiled or soaked.
Vitamin C is destroyed by prolonged heat, by light, by alkalis such as bicarbonate of soda, and by oxidation in air.
The enzyme oxidase is released when plant cells are cut or bruised and destroys vitamin C, so cut vegetables should be cooked promptly.
Copper and brass pans destroy vitamin C, and it is also lost during long storage and dehydration.
Vitamin C is an antioxidant, which means it acts as a reducing agent (it donates electrons), and this is how it changes ferric iron to ferrous iron.
notes.tip: For the Higher Level properties, learn the list: water-soluble, crystalline acid, unstable to heat, air, light, alkali, oxidase, copper and dehydration. For how vitamin C helps iron absorption, say it changes ferric iron to ferrous iron as a reducing agent.

notes.b: Vitamin B12 is unusual because only animal foods contain it naturally. Its absorption also needs a helper made in the stomach.
points: Vitamin B12 occurs naturally only in animal foods: liver and kidney, meat, fish and oily fish, eggs, milk, cheese and yoghurt.
Plant foods contain no natural vitamin B12, so vegans rely on fortified foods such as some breakfast cereals, plant milks and yeast extract, or on supplements.
The lining of the stomach makes intrinsic factor, a protein that binds vitamin B12 so that it can be absorbed in the ileum (the end of the small intestine).
The liver stores vitamin B12, and the store can last for several years, so deficiency develops slowly.
notes.tip: Expect vegan diet questions on B12: the answer is that plant foods have no natural B12, so fortified foods or supplements are needed.

notes.b: B12 is needed wherever cells are being made or nerves are working, which is why its deficiency affects both the blood and the nervous system.
points: Vitamin B12 works with folate to form healthy red blood cells.
Vitamin B12 is needed for the synthesis of DNA, so it is needed for cell division, especially in cells that divide rapidly.
Vitamin B12 maintains the myelin sheath, the fatty layer that insulates nerve fibres and keeps nerve impulses working normally, so it keeps nerve cells healthy.
Vitamin B12 is also involved in the body's use of fatty acids and amino acids.
notes.tip: Higher Level questions expect red blood cell formation and the nerve myelin sheath.

notes.b: A lack of B12 harms both the blood and the nerves. The cause can be the diet or a failure to absorb the vitamin.
points: B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia, in which red blood cells are too large and immature and cannot carry oxygen effectively.
Symptoms of this anaemia include tiredness, weakness, pale skin and breathlessness.
Nerve damage causes numbness and tingling in the hands and feet, poor balance and memory problems.
A strict vegan diet without fortified foods or supplements can cause deficiency.
Pernicious anaemia is the form of B12 deficiency caused by a lack of intrinsic factor, often through an autoimmune condition, which prevents B12 absorption even when the diet is adequate.
Failure to absorb B12 can also come from stomach or gut disease, and older people absorb less.
notes.tip: Pernicious anaemia is specifically B12 deficiency because intrinsic factor is missing; a vegan with a B12-poor diet has B12-deficiency (megaloblastic) anaemia, not strictly pernicious anaemia. Only B12 deficiency, not folate deficiency, damages nerves.

notes.h: Properties of vitamin B12 (Higher Level only)
notes.b: B12 is more stable than vitamin C, but it is not indestructible.
points: Vitamin B12 is water-soluble, so some is lost into cooking water.
Vitamin B12 is a red crystalline compound that contains the mineral cobalt, which gives it the name cobalamin.
Vitamin B12 is stable to heat in ordinary cooking but is destroyed by light and by strong acids and alkalis.

notes.b: Folate is the natural form of vitamin B9, and folic acid is the synthetic form. Folate is needed for making new cells, which matters most in early pregnancy.
points: Natural folate is found in dark green leafy vegetables such as spinach, broccoli, sprouts and cabbage, in pulses such as chickpeas, lentils and beans, and in asparagus, oranges, liver and yeast extract.
Wholegrain and fortified breakfast cereals also supply folate.
Folic acid is the synthetic form used in supplements and in fortified foods such as breakfast cereals. It is not a different vitamin from folate.
Folate is needed to synthesise DNA and RNA, so it is essential for cell division and growth, including the growth of the foetus.
Folate works with vitamin B12 to form red blood cells.

In the first weeks of pregnancy, folate is essential for the formation of the neural tube, the early brain and spinal cord, and it protects against neural tube defects such as spina bifida and anencephaly.
notes.tip: Questions ask for two or three functions of folate plus two sources: red blood cells, DNA and RNA synthesis, foetal development and preventing neural tube defects; green leafy vegetables, pulses, liver and fortified cereals.

notes.b: The neural tube forms in the first weeks of pregnancy, before many women know they are pregnant, so folate advice is aimed at women before they conceive.
points: A lack of folate causes megaloblastic anaemia, with the same large, immature red blood cells as B12 deficiency, and tiredness, weakness, pale skin, breathlessness and a sore tongue.
Neural tube defects, such as spina bifida and anencephaly, can develop in the unborn baby if the mother lacks folate in early pregnancy.
Poor growth is also an effect of folate deficiency.

Women who may become pregnant are advised, in HSE advice, to take a folic acid supplement before conception and during early pregnancy to reduce the risk of neural tube defects, as well as eating folate-rich foods.
notes.tip: Neural tube defect prevention by folic acid is asked as a gap-fill. Folate and B12 deficiency give the same type of anaemia, but only B12 deficiency damages nerves.

notes.b: Folate is fragile in the kitchen, which is why fortified foods use the more stable synthetic form.
points: Folate is water-soluble and is sensitive to heat, light and oxygen, so it is destroyed by prolonged cooking and storage.
Folate is lost into cooking water during prolonged boiling.
Synthetic folic acid is more stable than natural folate, which is why it is used in fortification.

keyTerms.definition: The chemical name for vitamin C, a water-soluble antioxidant needed for collagen formation.
A disease caused by severe, prolonged lack of vitamin C, with bleeding gums, loose teeth and slow wound healing.
The fibrous protein that gives strength to skin, blood vessels, gums, bones and teeth, and whose formation requires vitamin C.
The Fe³⁺ form of iron, which vitamin C reduces to the ferrous form before it can be absorbed.
The chemical name for vitamin B12, the water-soluble vitamin that contains cobalt and is found only in animal foods.
A protein made in the stomach that binds vitamin B12 so that it can be absorbed in the ileum.
An anaemia caused by failure to absorb vitamin B12 because intrinsic factor is missing, in which the red blood cells are large and unable to carry oxygen effectively.
A water-soluble B-group vitamin needed for DNA and RNA synthesis and for protecting the developing neural tube.
A birth defect of the brain or spinal cord, such as spina bifida, that folate in early pregnancy helps to prevent.
The loss of water-soluble vitamins and minerals from food into the cooking water.

questions.prompt: Explain how vitamin C helps the body absorb iron from a plant-based meal, and name two plant foods that are good sources of vitamin C.
questions.model: Vitamin C converts non-haem iron from the ferric (Fe³⁺) form to the ferrous (Fe²⁺) form, which is absorbed more readily in the small intestine. Two plant foods, any two of: citrus fruit, blackcurrants, kiwi, strawberries, peppers, broccoli, tomatoes, cabbage, new potatoes. Marks for the mechanism (conversion of ferric to ferrous, better absorption) and for each correct food.

questions.prompt: Discuss the sources, functions and effects of deficiency of vitamin B12 and folate, and explain why the two vitamins work together in the body.
questions.model: Vitamin B12: found only in animal foods such as liver, kidney, red meat, oily fish, eggs, milk and cheese; fortified foods supply it to vegans. Functions: forms healthy red blood cells with folate; maintains the myelin sheath around nerves; needed for DNA synthesis. Absorption needs intrinsic factor from the stomach. Deficiency: pernicious anaemia with large immature red blood cells, tiredness and pale skin; nerve damage with numbness and poor balance. Folate: natural folate in dark green leafy vegetables, pulses, asparagus, oranges and liver; folic acid in supplements and fortified cereals. Functions: synthesis of DNA and RNA for cell division and growth; protects the developing neural tube in early pregnancy. Deficiency: megaloblastic anaemia; neural tube defects such as spina bifida. Working together: both are needed to form healthy red blood cells, and a deficiency of either produces the same type of anaemia.
